bio:
Claude Monet (1840–1926) grew up in the Normandy port of Le Havre, where the landscape painter Eugène Boudin encouraged him to work outdoors. In Paris he joined Renoir, Sisley and Pissarro in pursuing fleeting effects of light and weather, and his canvas Impression, Sunrise gave the Impressionist movement its name when critics mocked it in 1874.

From 1883 Monet lived at Giverny, where he increasingly painted in series, returning to a single motif at different hours and seasons. The collection holds several of his Stacks of Wheat from 1890–91, including Stack of Wheat (Snow Effect, Overcast Day) and Stacks of Wheat (End of Day, Autumn), alongside Poppy Field (Giverny) and views of London such as Houses of Parliament and Waterloo Bridge, Gray Weather.

Earlier works trace the path to that approach: The Beach at Sainte-Adresse (1867), The Artist's House at Argenteuil (1873) and Arrival of the Normandy Train, Gare Saint-Lazare (1877). In his final decades Monet turned to the water garden he built at Giverny; Water Lily Pond and Irises show the loose, near-abstract painting that later generations of modernists admired.

Paul Gauguin (1848–1903) spent his early adulthood as a sailor and then a Paris stockbroker, painting on weekends and showing with the Impressionists before committing to art full time in the 1880s. In Brittany, at Pont-Aven, he and Émile Bernard developed a style of flat color areas and bold outlines meant to convey feeling and symbol rather than observed fact. Their collaborative Earthly Paradise reflects those experiments, and Arlésiennes (Mistral) comes from his turbulent weeks with Vincent van Gogh in Arles in 1888.

In 1891 Gauguin left for Tahiti in search of a life he imagined as untouched by European civilization. Paintings such as Te raau rahi (The Big Tree), Merahi metua no Tehamana and Mahana no atua (Day of the God) blend Polynesian subjects with invented mythology and saturated color. These works are now also read critically for their colonial fantasies. He died in the Marquesas Islands in 1903.

Gauguin also worked in ceramics and carved wood, as the Vase in the Form of a Tropical Plant with Bird and Deity and his Decorated Wooden Box show, and his free use of color and "primitive" sources shaped the Symbolists, the Fauves and early modernism.

Narcissa Niblack Thorne (1882–1966) was born in Vincennes, Indiana, and settled in Chicago after her marriage into the family behind the Montgomery Ward company. A lifelong collector of miniature furniture and accessories, she conceived a remarkable project in the 1930s: a series of historically accurate interiors built at a scale of one inch to one foot.

Working from her own research into period architecture and decoration, Thorne designed the rooms and had them executed by skilled craftsmen, with lighting and views through windows arranged like stage sets to make each space feel inhabited. The resulting 68 Thorne Miniature Rooms, now at the Art Institute of Chicago, span European interiors from the 13th century to the 1930s and American rooms from the 17th century onward.

This collection includes European rooms such as E1: English Great Room of the Late Tudor Period and E24: French Salon of the Louis XVI Period, and American rooms including A17: Pennsylvania Kitchen, 1752 and A33: "Middletown" Parlor, 1875–90, the latter a nod to her home state. Together they offer a compact survey of domestic design across four centuries.

John Singer Sargent (1856–1925) was born in Florence to American parents and grew up traveling across Europe. He trained in Paris under the portraitist Carolus-Duran and studied the fluid brushwork of Velázquez and Frans Hals, influences visible in early works here such as Venetian Glass Workers and Rehearsal of the Pasdeloup Orchestra at the Cirque d'Hiver.

After his Portrait of Madame X caused a scandal at the 1884 Salon, Sargent moved to London, where he became the most sought-after society portraitist of his generation on both sides of the Atlantic. Mrs. George Swinton, Mrs. Charles Gifford Dyer and Madame Paul Escudier show his ability to combine dazzling surface effects with a sharp sense of character; the collection also includes his portrait of Marion Deering, wife of one of his Chicago patrons.

Around 1907 Sargent largely gave up formal portraiture to paint landscapes, watercolors and mural decorations, notably for the Boston Public Library. Thistles, painted after his friendship with Claude Monet drew him outdoors, and The Fountain, Villa Torlonia, Frascati, Italy show this freer, sunlit side of his work.

Édouard Manet (1832–1883) was a Parisian from a well-off family who trained in the studio of Thomas Couture and absorbed the example of Spanish painters, above all Velázquez. His Le Déjeuner sur l'herbe, shown at the Salon des Refusés in 1863, and Olympia, exhibited in 1865, provoked outrage by treating modern subjects with frank, flattened handling, and made him a hero to the younger artists who became the Impressionists.

Manet never exhibited in the Impressionist group shows, preferring to fight for recognition at the official Salon, yet he is widely seen as a bridge between Realism and Impressionism. His brief trip to Spain in 1865 inspired Bullfight, while the paired Beggar with Oysters (Philosopher) and Beggar with a Duffle Coat (Philosopher) pay homage to Velázquez's portraits of philosophers.

The collection also shows his range across genres: the rushing horses of The Races at Longchamp, the Dutch-inspired Fish (Still Life), an early seascape and, from his last years, Woman Reading, a glimpse of modern Parisian café life painted with quick, luminous strokes.

name: Francisco Goya
bio:
Francisco Goya (1746–1828) rose from provincial Aragon to become First Court Painter to the Spanish crown. Early in his career he designed tapestry cartoons for the royal residences; the oil sketches Boy on a Ram and Winter Scene belong to that world of popular Spanish types and everyday incident.

A serious illness in 1792–93 left Goya deaf, and his art grew darker and more personal. Alongside official portraits he produced the satirical print series Los Caprichos and, after the Napoleonic invasion, The Disasters of War, a searing record of violence. His late "Black Paintings," made on the walls of his house outside Madrid, are among the most haunting images in European art.

The collection's six small panels telling the story of Friar Pedro and the bandit El Maragato show Goya working for his own pleasure on a real news event of 1806, when a monk overpowered a notorious outlaw. Read in sequence, from El Maragato Threatens Friar Pedro de Zaldivia with His Gun to Friar Pedro Binds El Maragato with a Rope, they unfold almost like a comic strip. Goya died in exile in Bordeaux, and he is often regarded as a forerunner of Romanticism and of modern art.

James McNeill Whistler (1834–1903) was born in Lowell, Massachusetts, but lived his entire adult life in Europe, moving between Paris, London and Venice. After a short spell at West Point he trained in Paris, then settled in London, where he became a celebrated and combative figure in the art world.

Whistler championed "art for art's sake," the idea that a painting should be judged by its harmony of color and form rather than its story. He gave his works musical titles such as "arrangements," "symphonies" and "nocturnes." Nocturne: Blue and Gold—Southampton Water is one of his hazy night views that pushed toward abstraction, and it was a similar nocturne that led to his famous 1878 libel suit against the critic John Ruskin.

The collection traces his development from Grey and Silver: Old Battersea Reach (1863) and Trouville (Grey and Green, the Silver Sea) to The Artist in His Studio, which reflects his fascination with Japanese art. A study for his Portrait of Thomas Carlyle, a companion to the famous portrait of his mother, and intimate panels like Coast Scene, Bathers show his refined, tonal approach at different scales.

Vincent van Gogh (1853–1890) came to art late, after working for an art dealer, as a teacher and as a lay preacher. He began painting around 1880 and in his first years in the Netherlands depicted rural laborers in dark earth tones, as in A Peasant Woman Digging in Front of Her Cottage.

In 1886 he joined his brother Theo, an art dealer, in Paris. There, exposed to Impressionism, Neo-Impressionism and Japanese prints, he brightened his palette and loosened his brushwork, seen here in Self-Portrait (1887), Fishing in Spring, the Pont de Clichy (Asnières) and Grapes, Lemons, Pears, and Apples.

In 1888 he moved to Arles in the south of France, hoping to found an artists' community, and briefly hosted Paul Gauguin. The Bedroom, one of three versions of his room in the Yellow House, and Madame Roulin Rocking the Cradle (La berceuse) belong to this intense period. After a breakdown he entered the asylum at Saint-Rémy, where he painted copies of artists he admired, such as The Drinkers after Honoré Daumier. He died in Auvers-sur-Oise in 1890, having sold little, and became one of the most influential painters of the modern era.

Giovanni Battista Tiepolo (1696–1770) was the leading Venetian painter of the 18th century and the last great master of grand decorative painting in the Baroque tradition. Working with astonishing speed and a light, luminous palette, he covered ceilings and walls with airy heavens full of gods, saints and allegorical figures.

His fame spread across Europe. He painted the celebrated frescoes of the Würzburg Residence in Germany in the early 1750s and spent his final years in Madrid decorating the Royal Palace for Charles III, dying there in 1770.

The collection's four large canvases of Rinaldo and Armida, painted around 1742–45 for a palace interior, illustrate Torquato Tasso's epic poem Jerusalem Delivered, in which a sorceress enchants a crusader knight. Beginning with Armida Encounters the Sleeping Rinaldo and ending with Rinaldo and the Magus of Ascalon, they show Tiepolo's gift for theatrical storytelling. The altarpiece Virgin and Child with Saints Dominic and Hyacinth reveals the same flair applied to religious devotion.

Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec (1864–1901) was born into an aristocratic family in Albi, in southern France. Two broken legs in his teens stopped his growth, likely because of an inherited condition, and he turned to art, training in Paris academic studios before settling in the bohemian district of Montmartre.

He became the great chronicler of Parisian nightlife, painting dancers, singers, performers and patrons of cafés, cabarets and circuses with sharp observation and a draftsman's economy of line. His color lithograph posters for venues such as the Moulin Rouge transformed commercial art and remain some of the most recognizable images of the period.

In the collection, Moulin de la Galette (1889) marked his arrival as a painter of dance-hall life, and At the Moulin Rouge gathers the club's regulars, and the artist himself, into a crowded, slightly eerie scene. Equestrienne (At the Cirque Fernando) and At the Circus: The Bareback Rider reflect his love of the circus, while the early Portrait of Jeanne Wenz shows his skill as a portraitist. Weakened by alcoholism, he died at 36.

name: Edgar Degas
bio:
Edgar Degas (1834–1917) was born into a Parisian banking family and trained in the classical tradition, admiring Ingres and copying Old Masters in Italy. His early ambition was history painting, as in Young Spartan Girls Challenging Boys, but by the late 1860s he had turned to modern life.

Degas helped organize the Impressionist exhibitions and showed in most of them, though he preferred to call himself a realist and disliked painting outdoors. He was fascinated by movement and by off-center, photographic compositions. Ballet dancers became his most famous subject, and Yellow Dancers (In the Wings) and On the Stage capture performers from unexpected angles, often in pastel, a medium he pushed to new expressive heights.

He was also a penetrating portraitist. Henri Degas and His Niece Lucie Degas records his own family with quiet psychological tension, and The Millinery Shop reflects his interest in working women and the fashion trades of Paris. In later life, with failing eyesight, he turned increasingly to sculpture, including the celebrated Little Dancer Aged Fourteen.

name: Paul Cézanne
bio:
Paul Cézanne (1839–1906) was born in Aix-en-Provence, where he was a boyhood friend of the novelist Émile Zola. After a difficult start in Paris, he worked alongside Camille Pissarro in the early 1870s, adopting a lighter palette and painting outdoors; Auvers, Panoramic View dates from this formative period, and he showed in the first and third Impressionist exhibitions.

Cézanne soon moved beyond Impressionism's fleeting effects, seeking a sense of structure and permanence. He built forms with patches of color and was willing to tilt tables, shift viewpoints and leave canvases looking unfinished if it served the composition. The Plate of Apples and The Vase of Tulips show this rethinking of the still life, while his repeated views of Mont Sainte-Victoire did the same for landscape.

Working largely in isolation in Provence, he returned again and again to the theme of bathers, as in Standing Bather, Seen from the Back and The Bathers (1899–1904). Recognition came late, but his approach proved decisive for Cubism and for Picasso, Matisse and generations of modern painters.

Peter Paul Rubens (1577–1640) was the leading painter of Baroque Flanders. Raised in Antwerp, he spent eight years in Italy studying ancient sculpture and the works of Titian, Michelangelo and Caravaggio before returning home in 1608 to become court painter to the Habsburg governors of the Southern Netherlands.

Rubens ran a large, efficient workshop and produced altarpieces, mythologies, portraits and vast decorative cycles for patrons across Europe. A learned man, he also served as a diplomat and was knighted by the kings of both Spain and England. His paintings are known for energetic movement, rich color and full-bodied figures.

The collection shows his working methods. The Capture of Samson is a vivid oil sketch for a larger painting; St. Albert of Louvain is one of the studies he made for the ceiling of the Jesuit church in Antwerp, later lost to fire; and The Adoration of the Eucharist was designed for a tapestry series for a convent in Madrid. The Holy Family with Saints Elizabeth and John the Baptist and Saint Francis reveal the warmth and devotion of his religious works.

Winslow Homer (1836–1910) was born in Boston and began his career as a commercial illustrator, working for Harper's Weekly and covering the Civil War from the front. In the late 1860s he turned to oil painting, and early works such as Croquet Scene and Mount Washington depict Americans at leisure with fresh, direct observation and strong outdoor light.

A stay in the English fishing village of Cullercoats in 1881–82 deepened his interest in people who lived by the sea. In 1883 he settled at Prouts Neck on the Maine coast, where he lived in relative isolation and painted the struggle between humans and nature. The Herring Net, showing two fishermen hauling a catch in a heavy swell, and Coast of Maine, with waves breaking over rocks, are characteristic of this mature period.

Homer was also a brilliant watercolorist, and his travels to the Adirondacks, Florida and the Caribbean produced some of the finest American works in that medium. Largely self-taught, he is widely regarded as one of the foremost American painters of the 19th century.

Auguste Rodin (1840–1917) is often called the father of modern sculpture. Rejected three times by the École des Beaux-Arts, he spent years working as a craftsman for decorative sculptors before a trip to Italy in 1875, where he studied Michelangelo, transformed his art.

In 1880 the French state commissioned him to design a bronze portal for a planned museum of decorative arts. Inspired by Dante's Inferno, The Gates of Hell occupied Rodin for the rest of his life and generated many independent figures, including The Thinker, The Kiss and the Adam and Eve after the Fall in this collection.

Rodin modeled surfaces that catch light and suggest movement and emotion, and he was willing to present fragments as finished works. The Walking Man, a headless and armless striding figure, shows this radical approach. His Portrait of Balzac relates to his monument to the novelist, rejected by the writers' society that commissioned it in 1898 and now seen as a landmark of modern sculpture.

Camille Pissarro (1830–1903) was born on the Caribbean island of St. Thomas, then part of the Danish West Indies, and moved to Paris in 1855 to become a painter. Influenced at first by Camille Corot, he developed a more robust approach, as in The Banks of the Marne in Winter, shown at the Salon of 1866.

During the Franco-Prussian War he took refuge near London, where he painted The Crystal Palace and studied English landscape painting with Claude Monet. Back in France, living in Pontoise and later Éragny, he became a central figure of Impressionism and the only artist to exhibit in all eight of the group's exhibitions. Rabbit Warren at Pontoise, Snow is one of the many snow scenes he painted.

Pissarro was a generous mentor, advising Cézanne, Gauguin and others, and he remained open to new ideas, briefly adopting the dot technique of Seurat's Neo-Impressionism in the late 1880s. Rural life and working people were constant themes, as in the late Woman Bathing Her Feet in a Brook (1895).

George Inness (1825–1894) was one of the most important American landscape painters of the 19th century. Born near Newburgh, New York, he began in the tradition of the Hudson River School, but trips to Europe introduced him to the French Barbizon painters, whose looser, more intimate approach to nature he embraced. Catskill Mountains (1870) shows a cultivated landscape shaped by human presence rather than untamed wilderness.

Inness was deeply influenced by the spiritual writings of Emanuel Swedenborg and came to see landscape as a way of expressing unseen realities. Over time his work grew softer and more atmospheric, dissolving detail into color and mood, an approach sometimes linked to American Tonalism.

A Marine, painted during a stay in Europe in the 1870s, shows his energetic handling of a stormy sea, while late works such as The Mill Pond (1889) and Early Morning, Tarpon Springs (1892), painted near his winter home in Florida, capture the hazy, poetic light that defines his mature style. He died in 1894 while traveling in Scotland.

Katsushika Hokusai (1760–1849) was one of the most prolific and inventive artists of Edo-period Japan. Over a career of about seventy years he produced paintings, book illustrations and thousands of designs for woodblock prints, working under some thirty different artistic names.

His most famous work, Under the Wave off Kanagawa, better known as The Great Wave, comes from the series Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji, published in the early 1830s. These landscape prints helped establish landscape as a major genre of ukiyo-e, a field previously dominated by actors and beauties. His multi-volume sketchbooks, the Hokusai Manga, recorded everything from wildlife to daily life.

The collection's four prints come from the series One Hundred Ghost Tales (Hyaku monogatari) of 1831–32, of which only a handful of designs were issued. Kohada Koheiji, Oiwa, The Mansion of the Plates and The Laughing Demoness draw on popular ghost stories and Kabuki plays with memorable, macabre invention. Hokusai's work later had a profound influence on European artists, including the Impressionists.

Tiffany and Company was founded in New York City in 1837 by Charles Lewis Tiffany and John B. Young as a shop for stationery and fancy goods. Within a few decades it had become one of America's leading jewelers and silversmiths, known for technical excellence and ambitious design.

Under the direction of silversmith Edward C. Moore, Tiffany's silver department drew freely on sources from ancient Greece to Japan and the Islamic world, and the firm won international acclaim at the Paris Exposition Universelle of 1878. The Saracenic Coffee Pot and Sugar Bowl (1895), inspired by Islamic metalwork, reflects this eclectic, globally minded approach. Charles Lewis Tiffany's son, Louis Comfort Tiffany, later became famous for his own work in stained glass and decorative arts.

The collection's Punch Bowl, Pair of Wine Coolers and Pair of Candelabra (1873) were commissioned by the United States government as a gift to Brazil's Viscount d'Itajubá, thanking him for his role in the arbitration between the United States and Great Britain after the Civil War. Their classical imagery of agriculture and commerce celebrates national prosperity.

name: El Greco
bio:
El Greco (1541–1614), born Doménikos Theotokópoulos on the island of Crete, trained as a painter of Byzantine icons before moving to Venice, where he absorbed the rich color of Titian and Tintoretto, and then to Rome. His nickname, "the Greek," stayed with him for life.

In 1577 he settled in Toledo, Spain, where he spent the rest of his career. The Assumption of the Virgin (1577–79), the centerpiece of an altarpiece for the convent of Santo Domingo el Antiguo, was his first major Spanish commission, and it announced a bold new voice. Over the following decades his style became ever more personal, with elongated figures, flickering light and unnaturally intense color that conveyed spiritual fervor.

Works such as Saint Francis Kneeling in Meditation and Saint Martin and the Beggar reflect the devotional climate of Counter-Reformation Spain, and El Greco produced many versions of both subjects for eager patrons. Largely forgotten after his death, he was rediscovered in the late 19th century and admired by modern artists, including Picasso and the Expressionists.

Eugène Delacroix (1798–1863) was the leading figure of French Romanticism. Against the cool, linear classicism championed by Ingres, he emphasized vivid color, dynamic brushwork and dramatic emotion. Works such as The Death of Sardanapalus and Liberty Leading the People, painted after the revolution of 1830, made him both celebrated and controversial.

Delacroix drew inspiration from literature, especially Shakespeare, Dante and Lord Byron. The Combat of the Giaour and Hassan (1826) is based on one of Byron's "oriental tales," a popular genre of the day. In 1832 he traveled with a French diplomatic mission to Morocco and briefly to Algeria, and the experience supplied him with subjects for decades.

The late works in the collection, Arab Horseman Attacked by a Lion and Lion Hunt, show his fascination with violent struggle between humans and animals, rendered in swirling, energetic compositions. These North African themes are now also viewed through the lens of 19th-century Orientalism. Delacroix's expressive use of color strongly influenced the Impressionists and Post-Impressionists, including Van Gogh and Cézanne.

Henry Fuseli (1741–1825) was born Johann Heinrich Füssli in Zurich and trained for the church before a career in literature and art took him to London. Encouraged by Joshua Reynolds, he spent eight years in Italy in the 1770s studying Michelangelo, and Two Heads of Damned Souls from Dante's "Inferno" dates from that period.

Returning to England, Fuseli caused a sensation with The Nightmare (1781), a dreamlike image of a sleeping woman and a crouching demon that remains his best-known work. He favored dramatic, exaggerated figures and supernatural or literary themes drawn from Shakespeare, Milton and Dante, anticipating Romanticism's fascination with the irrational.

Milton Dictating to His Daughter (1794) relates to his ambitious Milton Gallery, a series of paintings on the poet's work. The Sketch for "Oath on the Rütli" prepared a painting of the legendary founding of the Swiss Confederation for his native Zurich. Fuseli became Professor of Painting and Keeper at the Royal Academy in London, and his work influenced his friend William Blake.

Marsden Hartley (1877–1943) was born in Lewiston, Maine, and became one of the pioneering American modernists. In the early 1910s he exhibited at Alfred Stieglitz's gallery 291 in New York, a key venue for avant-garde art, and Stieglitz helped fund his travels to Europe.

Unlike most Americans, Hartley was drawn more to German Expressionism than to French art. In Berlin he came into contact with the Blue Rider circle around Vasily Kandinsky and Franz Marc, and he painted bold, emblematic compositions. Movement (1913), with its vibrant, rhythmic abstraction, belongs to this period.

Returning to the United States, Hartley sought subjects in American landscape. The Last of New England—The Beginning of New Mexico and Landscape No. 3, Cash Entry Mines, New Mexico come from his stay in the Southwest in 1918–20, where the dramatic terrain inspired dense, sculptural forms. In his last years he returned to Maine, painting its coast, mountains and people with blunt, expressive power.

Mary Cassatt (1844–1926) was born near Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, and studied at the Pennsylvania Academy of the Fine Arts before moving to Europe to continue her training. After travels in Italy and Spain, where she painted subjects such as After the Bullfight (1873), she settled permanently in Paris.

Edgar Degas admired her work and invited her to exhibit with the Impressionists; she was the only American to do so, first showing with the group in 1879. On a Balcony, shown in their 1880 exhibition, displays her energetic brushwork and bright palette.

Cassatt is best known for sensitive, unsentimental images of women's private lives and of mothers and children, such as The Child's Bath (1893). Inspired by Japanese woodblock prints, she also produced innovative color prints. She played a major role in bringing Impressionism to the United States, advising American collectors, notably Louisine and Henry Havemeyer, whose purchases now enrich several American museums.

Pierre-Auguste Renoir (1841–1919) was born in Limoges and began working as a painter of porcelain before studying art in Paris. In the studio of Charles Gleyre he met Claude Monet, Alfred Sisley and Frédéric Bazille, and together they developed the techniques that would become Impressionism, painting outdoors with broken touches of bright color.

Renoir loved people more than landscapes, and his best-known works depict Parisians at leisure, such as Dance at the Moulin de la Galette and Luncheon of the Boating Party. Young Woman Sewing, whose model may be his future wife Aline Charigot, and Acrobats at the Cirque Fernando (Francisca and Angelina Wartenberg), both from 1879, glow with warm light and feathery brushwork.

Two Sisters (On the Terrace) of 1881 is one of his most celebrated paintings, shown at the seventh Impressionist exhibition in 1882. In the following years Renoir moved toward firmer drawing inspired by Renaissance art. Despite severe rheumatoid arthritis in later life, he kept painting until his death at Cagnes-sur-Mer in 1919.

Piet Mondrian (1872–1944) was born in Amersfoort in the Netherlands and trained as a traditional landscape painter. The flat Dutch countryside, with its horizon lines, canals and windmills, remained a touchstone for him, and Farm near Duivendrecht (c. 1916) shows how he simplified such motifs into rhythmic patterns of line and tone.

After encountering Cubism in Paris before World War I, Mondrian moved steadily toward pure abstraction. In 1917 he co-founded the movement De Stijl (The Style) with Theo van Doesburg, and he developed a philosophy he called Neo-Plasticism, reducing painting to horizontal and vertical black lines, the primary colors and white, gray and black.

Lozenge Composition with Yellow, Black, Blue, Red, and Gray (1921), a square canvas turned on its point, and Composition (No. 1) Gray-Red (1935) show his quest for a universal visual harmony. Fleeing war, he moved to London in 1938 and New York in 1940, where the city's energy inspired late works such as Broadway Boogie Woogie. He died in New York in 1944.

Alfred Sisley (1839–1899) was born in Paris to English parents and remained a British citizen all his life, although he lived and worked almost entirely in France. He studied in the studio of Charles Gleyre, where he met Monet, Renoir and Bazille, and became one of the founding members of the Impressionist group.

Sisley devoted himself almost exclusively to landscape, especially the rivers, villages and changing skies of the Île-de-France. His family's business collapsed after the Franco-Prussian War, and he spent much of his career in financial hardship, moving between villages west and south of Paris.

The collection's two paintings date from 1875, when he lived in Marly-le-Roi. Watering Place at Marly shows the pool beside his home, while The Seine at Port-Marly, Piles of Sand captures workers dredging the river, a reminder that Impressionist landscapes often included modern labor and industry. Sisley later settled in Moret-sur-Loing, where he died in 1899, shortly before his work began to achieve real market success.

Berthe Morisot (1841–1895) was born in Bourges into a cultured family and studied painting in Paris, including informal guidance from Camille Corot. She exhibited at the official Salon in the 1860s before joining the Impressionists, and she showed in all but one of their eight exhibitions, missing only the year her daughter Julie was born.

In 1874 Morisot married Eugène Manet, brother of the painter Édouard Manet, with whom she had a long artistic friendship. As a woman of her class, she had limited access to the cafés and public spaces her male colleagues painted, and she focused instead on domestic interiors, gardens and the lives of women and children.

Her technique was among the freest of the group. Woman at Her Toilette, rendered with feathery strokes in lavender, pink and white, and Woman in a Garden, where figure and foliage dissolve into the same flickering brushwork, show how she treated figures almost as landscapes. Long overshadowed by her male peers, Morisot is now recognized as a central figure of Impressionism.

Georges Seurat (1859–1891) trained at the École des Beaux-Arts in Paris, where he studied drawing in the academic tradition. He also read scientific writings on color and optics, including the theories of Michel-Eugène Chevreul, and set out to put Impressionism's intuitive approach to color on a more systematic footing.

His first major painting, Bathers at Asnières, was rejected by the Salon of 1884 and shown instead with the newly formed Society of Independent Artists. The Final Study for "Bathers at Asnières" in this collection shows how carefully he planned its calm, monumental composition.

Seurat then developed the technique known as Pointillism or Divisionism, applying small dots of pure color intended to blend in the viewer's eye. A Sunday on La Grande Jatte — 1884, his largest and most famous work, took two years to complete and caused a stir at the final Impressionist exhibition in 1886. It launched Neo-Impressionism, followed by artists such as Paul Signac. Seurat died suddenly at just 31, leaving a small but hugely influential body of work.

Gustave Caillebotte (1848–1894) came from a wealthy Parisian family and studied law and engineering before training as a painter. His fortune allowed him to act as a patron of the Impressionists, buying works by his friends, helping to finance their exhibitions and organizing several of them.

His own paintings combine Impressionist subjects with sharper drawing and bold, often plunging perspectives. His scenes of the rebuilt boulevards of Paris, and of working men such as The Floor Scrapers, captured the modern city with unusual precision.

Paris Street; Rainy Day, shown at the third Impressionist exhibition in 1877, is his masterpiece: a large, crisply rendered view of a newly built intersection, with umbrella-carrying pedestrians arranged with near-photographic clarity. Calf's Head and Ox Tongue, a stark still life of butcher's cuts, shows his interest in unconventional subjects. Caillebotte left his collection to the French state, and the bequest, including works by Monet, Renoir, Cézanne and others, became a cornerstone of the national Impressionist collections now at the Musée d'Orsay.

Henri Matisse (1869–1954) was born in northern France and worked as a law clerk before discovering painting while recovering from an illness. He studied in Paris under Gustave Moreau and absorbed lessons from Cézanne, Gauguin and the Neo-Impressionists.

In 1905 Matisse and his circle exhibited canvases of such startling, non-naturalistic color that a critic called them "fauves" (wild beasts), and Matisse became the leader of Fauvism. Over the following decades he pursued an art of balance and expressive color, and he is regarded, with Picasso, as one of the defining artists of the 20th century.

Matisse also worked seriously as a sculptor. The Serf, one of his earliest sculptures, was modeled from a man who had also posed for Rodin and reveals his search for a personal style. Apples (1916), painted during World War I, reflects a period of experimentation with more austere, structured compositions. In later life, living in Nice and confined by illness, he created his celebrated cut-outs from painted paper.

name: Jacques-Louis David
bio:
Jacques-Louis David (1748–1825) was the leading painter of French Neoclassicism. After winning the Prix de Rome in 1774 he studied in Italy, where ancient sculpture and the paintings of Poussin shaped his clear, severe style. The Oath of the Horatii (1784–85) became a manifesto for an art of civic virtue, clean lines and sober color, in reaction against the playful Rococo.

David was also a revolutionary. He sat in the National Convention, voted for the execution of Louis XVI and painted The Death of Marat as a secular martyrdom. Later he became First Painter to Napoleon, recording his coronation in a vast canvas. After the restoration of the monarchy he went into exile in Brussels, where he died.

The collection shows his intimate side as a portraitist. Madame François Buron (1769) depicts the aunt who helped raise him, and Madame de Pastoret and Her Son, left unfinished, likely because of the upheavals of the Revolution, offers a rare view of his working process.

Sandro Botticelli (c. 1445–1510) was one of the leading painters of early Renaissance Florence. He trained with Fra Filippo Lippi and developed a style of graceful, rhythmic line and delicate, idealized figures. His work found favor with the Medici family and their circle, and in 1481–82 he was among the artists summoned to paint frescoes on the walls of the Sistine Chapel in Rome.

Botticelli is best known today for mythological paintings such as Primavera and The Birth of Venus, which reflect the humanist culture of Medici Florence. Yet much of his output was devotional, and he and his workshop produced many images of the Virgin and Child for private homes.

Virgin and Child with an Angel and Virgin and Child with Two Angels show his tender, melancholy vision of Mary and the infant Jesus. In his later years, influenced by the preacher Girolamo Savonarola, his religious work became more intense. Botticelli fell into obscurity after his death and was rediscovered in the 19th century.

Utagawa Hiroshige (1797–1858) was one of the last great masters of the Japanese woodblock print. Born into a family of fire wardens in Edo (now Tokyo), he trained with the Utagawa school and first designed prints of actors and beauties before finding his calling in landscape.

His breakthrough came with The Fifty-three Stations of the Tōkaidō (1833–34), recording scenes along the highway linking Edo and Kyoto. Where Hokusai's landscapes are dynamic and inventive, Hiroshige's are lyrical and atmospheric, capturing weather, seasons and the moods of travel with subtle color.

The collection's two prints come from his final masterpiece, One Hundred Famous Views of Edo (1856–58), a series notable for dramatic vertical compositions and striking foregrounds. New Year's Eve Fox Fires at the Changing Tree depicts a folk belief that foxes gathered at a tree near Ōji on the last night of the year, and The Pine of Success and Onmayagashi, Asakusa River shows the Sumida River at dusk. Hiroshige's work captivated European artists; Van Gogh copied two prints from this series.

Vasily Kandinsky (1866–1944) was born in Moscow and trained in law and economics before abandoning an academic career at 30 to study painting in Munich. His early work drew on Russian folk art and fairy tales, and Painting with Troika (1911) still carries echoes of the traditional three-horse sleigh.

A pioneer of abstract art, Kandinsky believed that color and form could affect the viewer directly, much as music does. In 1911 he and Franz Marc founded the Blue Rider (Der Blaue Reiter), a loose association of artists in Munich, and he published Concerning the Spiritual in Art, a key text of modernism. Improvisation No. 30 (Cannons) (1913) shows his move toward abstraction, although traces of cannons and buildings remain.

World War I forced Kandinsky back to Russia. In 1922 he joined the Bauhaus in Germany, teaching there until the Nazis closed the school in 1933. He then moved to France and spent his final years near Paris, continuing to develop a vocabulary of geometric and organic forms.

Thomas Cole (1801–1848) was born in Lancashire, England, and emigrated with his family to the United States in 1818. Largely self-taught, he made sketching trips up the Hudson River in the 1820s, and his paintings of the Catskill Mountains attracted the attention of New York collectors and artists.

Cole is considered the founder of the Hudson River School, the first significant American landscape movement. His paintings celebrate the grandeur of the American wilderness and often carry moral or religious meaning. He also painted ambitious allegorical series such as The Course of Empire and The Voyage of Life, and The Oxbow contrasts wild and cultivated land.

Distant View of Niagara Falls (1830) captures an already iconic American landmark, which Cole had visited in 1829, while New England Scenery (1839) presents a peaceful pastoral view of farms and villages set against distant mountains. Settling in the town of Catskill, New York, he trained the young Frederic Edwin Church, and his influence shaped American landscape painting for decades.

William Merritt Chase (1849–1916) was born in Indiana and trained in New York and at the Royal Academy in Munich, where he absorbed a dark, bravura painting style inspired by Frans Hals and Velázquez. Returning to New York in 1878, he took a famous studio in the Tenth Street Studio Building and furnished it lavishly, making it a meeting place for artists and patrons.

Over time Chase lightened his palette and embraced Impressionist techniques. A City Park, probably depicting Brooklyn's Tompkins Park, captures the sparkle of a summer day with a bold, empty diagonal walkway. He painted scenes of urban parks, elegant interiors and still lifes with fluid, confident brushwork.

Chase was one of the most influential art teachers in American history. From 1891 to 1902 he led the Shinnecock Hills Summer School on Long Island, where students painted outdoors; Wind-Swept Sands (1894) shows the dunes of that region under gray skies. His many students included Georgia O'Keeffe, Edward Hopper and Charles Demuth.

Childe Hassam (1859–1935) was born in Dorchester, Massachusetts, and began his career as an illustrator in Boston. Studying at the Académie Julian in Paris in the late 1880s, he encountered French Impressionism, and he became one of its most dedicated American practitioners.

Hassam painted bustling city streets in Boston, Paris and New York, as well as sunny coastal scenes. In 1897 he was a founding member of the Ten American Painters, a group that broke away from established art societies to exhibit Impressionist-inspired work. During World War I he produced his celebrated series of flag paintings of New York's Fifth Avenue.

For many summers Hassam visited Appledore Island in the Isles of Shoals off the New Hampshire coast, where the poet Celia Thaxter hosted artists and writers and cultivated a famous garden. The Little Pond, Appledore (1890) comes from these visits. New England Headlands (1899) depicts Gloucester, Massachusetts, a popular summer artists' colony, with broken brushwork and bright, clear light.

Frederic Remington (1861–1909) was born in Canton, New York, and studied briefly at the Yale School of Fine Arts before heading west in the early 1880s. He worked as a sheep rancher and traveled widely through the western territories, sketching cowboys, soldiers and Native Americans.

Remington found fame as an illustrator for magazines such as Harper's Weekly, and his dramatic images shaped how Americans imagined the frontier. His paintings present mythic, romanticized views of the West at a time when that frontier was rapidly disappearing, and they are now also read critically for their portrayal of Native Americans.

The Advance-Guard, or The Military Sacrifice (1890) shows a cavalry scout ambushed on the plains. In 1895 Remington turned to sculpture, and The Bronco Buster, his first bronze, depicting a cowboy clinging to a rearing horse, became one of the most popular American sculptures ever made. He went on to create more than twenty bronzes before his early death at the age of 48.

Robert Henri (1865–1929) was born Robert Henry Cozad in Cincinnati, Ohio; his family changed their names after his father was involved in a fatal shooting. He studied at the Pennsylvania Academy of the Fine Arts and in Paris, and admired the direct, vigorous painting of Frans Hals, Velázquez and Manet.

Henri became the leader of a group of Philadelphia and New York artists who rejected genteel academic art in favor of scenes of everyday urban life. In 1908 he organized the landmark exhibition of The Eight at New York's Macbeth Gallery, and his circle became associated with what was later called the Ashcan School.

He was also an inspiring teacher whose students included Edward Hopper, George Bellows and Stuart Davis, and his ideas were collected in the book The Art Spirit (1923). Himself and Herself (1913) were painted during a summer in Ireland and portray the fisherman Johnnie Cummings and his wife, Biddy, with thick, lush paint and informal, forthright poses.
